title: I have seen thy tears (2 Kings 20:1–6)
hookLine: told he will die, Hezekiah turns to the wall and weeps, and is given fifteen years
carry: the weeping was part of the prayer
last: LAY IT OPEN BEFORE YOU ANSWER.

cards: Set your house in order, "for thou shalt die, and not live." That's what the prophet Isaiah says at the bedside of King Hezekiah, who is sick, the text says, unto death. No softening.
No second opinion. It comes from the prophet himself, in the name of God. Some news closes a door so firmly that there seems nothing left to say.
What Hezekiah does next is a small movement of the body you can almost see.

teach.h: HE TURNED HIS FACE TO THE WALL.
teach.b: He turns his face to the wall, away from the room, with the prophet still standing there.
And he prays, short and honest: remember now how I have walked before you in truth and with a whole heart, and done what is good in your sight.
Then the text adds: Hezekiah wept sore. Now watch the speed of what follows. Before Isaiah has even made it out of the courtyard, the word of the Lord comes to him: turn back.

teach.h: HEARD THY PRAYER, SEEN THY TEARS.
teach.b: Tell Hezekiah, "I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears". I will heal you. On the third day you'll go up to the house of the Lord, and I will add to your days fifteen years.
Notice the pair: heard and seen. God hears the words and also sees the tears. The weeping isn't treated as weakness or a failure of faith.
It is part of the prayer, the part that gets seen.

teach.h: A SWORD ON THE NECK, STILL ASK.
teach.b: The Talmud tells a version of this scene in which Hezekiah answers Isaiah with a teaching from his ancestors' house: even when a sharp sword rests on a person's neck, they should not hold back from asking for mercy.
The verdict sounded final. He prayed anyway. Why did the decree change?
The text doesn't explain, and readers have argued about it. What it does make plain is the picture: a man facing the wall, crying, and a God who notices the tears.

how: Jews read Hezekiah's illness in the book of Kings and again in Isaiah 38, and the Talmud draws from it the teaching that a person keeps asking for mercy even when things look hopeless.

games.q: you're Hezekiah. the prophet has just said you will die, and not live. what do you do?
o: accept it in silence and set your affairs in order.
turn your face to the wall, pray and weep.
games.why: he turns to the wall, prays, and weeps sore. before Isaiah leaves the courtyard, God answers: I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears.

practice: Bring to mind some news that felt like a closed door, a diagnosis, a rejection, a no, and if it helps, turn slightly away from the room, the way Hezekiah turned to the wall.

Say silently what's true, what you've tried and what you hope, and if tears come, let them; they're allowed here. If you pray, you can ask for mercy even now; if you don't, just speak honestly, even after the news.
